To describe a town and the memories connected with it.
A walk around Sibiu
August. Matei and Giulia landed in Sibiu last night. In the morning Matei shows Giulia the town.
Here's the Great Square. It's the square where I used to play as a child.
It's gorgeous! And those little windows on the roofs? They look like eyes!
They really are "the eyes of the town". People say they're always watching you. They're the thing tourists take the most photos of.
And that iron bridge I can see down there?
It's the Bridge of Lies. According to legend, whoever tells a lie on the bridge makes it collapse.
Then let's go! I'll ask you a question you have to answer honestly.
Hmm… All right. What do you want to know?
How many girls have you brought onto this bridge before me?
None. You're the first person I've shown Sibiu to like this.
(looks at the bridge) The bridge is still standing. So it's true!
Come on, I'll show you the school I went to and the house where I grew up.
And tonight I'll meet your parents. That's what scares me most!
Relax. My mother has already cooked for ten people. Whatever you don't eat, she'll give you to take back to Florence.

CUI = "kooee", one syllable: in CUI, a CUI.
Careful: bu-JEE-e (GI = "jee"), led-JEN-da (GG = a long "j").
SCI + u = "sh": kre-SHOO-to. And "crescere" = KRE-she-re.
QUA = "kwa": KWA-le, il KWA-le, la KWA-le.
1. CHE: subject or direct object
CHE is the most common relative. It replaces a subject or a direct object and NEVER changes (neither gender nor number):
subject
La ragazza che parla è Giulia.
The girl who's talking is Giulia.
I tetti che guardano la piazza.
The roofs that look over the square.
Il ponte che vedi è famoso.
The bridge you can see is famous.
Le foto che ho fatto.
In Romanian we say "pe care îl vezi" (with a doubled pronoun). In Italian just "che vedi" — no "lo"! Not "il ponte che lo vedi".
2. CUI: after a preposition
After any preposition (a, di, da, in, con, su, per, tra) you use CUI, which doesn't change either:
la casa in cui sono nato
the house where I was born
la ragazza di cui ti ho parlato
the girl I told you about
l'amico a cui scrivo
the friend I'm writing to
la ragione per cui sono qui
the reason why I'm here
le persone con cui lavoro
the people I work with
il tavolo su cui mangiamo
the table we eat at
"A cui" can drop the "a": "la persona cui ho scritto" — but it's rarer. Simpler: always use "a cui".
3. IL QUALE, LA QUALE, I QUALI, LE QUALI
The formal version of CHE and CUI. It agrees with the noun and merges with the preposition (al quale, della quale, nei quali…). It's useful when CHE would be ambiguous:
Matei's sister, who lives in Sibiu, is a doctor.
The professor I wrote to hasn't answered.
The friends I left with.
In speech Italians almost always prefer CHE and CUI. IL QUALE appears mostly in writing and official language.
4. QUELLO CHE / CIÒ CHE = what
Do what you like.
All I have is yours.
Not "che" alone meaning "what": "Non capisco che dici" is colloquial / wrong in writing. Correct: "quello che dici".
5. CHI = whoever, the one who
CHI means "the one who / whoever" and takes a SINGULAR verb. It's very common in proverbs:
Proverb / phrase
Chi dorme non piglia pesci.
The early bird catches the worm. (lit. Whoever sleeps catches no fish.)
Chi va piano va sano e va lontano.
Slow and steady wins the race.
Chi trova un amico trova un tesoro.
Whoever finds a friend finds a treasure.
Chi vuole venire è il benvenuto.
Anyone who wants to come is welcome.

Lettera da Sibiu

"Dear Graziella, I'm writing to you from the room where Matei slept as a boy. On the walls there are still the posters he put up at fifteen: a rock band I've never heard of and a print of Botticelli's Primavera. Even back then, you see.

Let me tell you about the evening I was so afraid of. We arrived at his parents' house at seven. His mother, Doina, opened the door — a small lady with eyes exactly like Matei's. Before she said a word to me, she hugged me so tight I couldn't breathe.

His father, Ion, is a tall, quiet man who worked as an engineer for the railways. He shook my hand, looked at me for a long time and then said in Italian, with a terrible accent: 'Welcome. You eat?' It was the only sentence he had learned, and he had learned it for me.

Then there was the grandmother, who is eighty-six and speaks no language but Romanian, yet I talked with her for an hour. I don't know how. She showed me photos, I pointed, she laughed. I understood everything that mattered.

And then the dinner! Graziella, you who are the best cook in the world, you should know you have a rival. On the table there were at least twelve dishes: the sarmale Ilinca had told us about, a sour soup called ciorbă, polenta with cheese and sour cream, chicken, the grandmother's cakes… Ion poured pălincă into the glasses and said: 'Noroc!' I found out it means 'cheers' and also 'luck'.

Ilinca arrived from the hospital at nine, still in her white coat. She sat next to me and whispered in my ear: 'Mum adores you. Dad has talked more tonight than in the whole year. The dog has already chosen you.' And indeed Lupu, the old dog Matei always tells me about, was asleep on my feet.

At the end of dinner Doina brought out a box. Inside were the drawings Matei made as a child: houses, bridges, churches, and a little portrait of a girl with curly black hair. 'He drew it when he was ten,' Ilinca explained. 'He said it was the girl he would marry.'

Matei went as red as the ciorbă. I looked at the drawing for a long time. Graziella, you won't believe it, but that little girl was wearing a green dress. Like the one I wore at my party, the evening the neighbour's dog dirtied his shirt.

Tomorrow we're leaving for the mountains Matei has been talking about for months. I've bought hiking boots that already hurt. Say hello to Pietro, Michelangelo and Signor Franco for me. And tell Pietro the Bridge of Lies is still standing. He'll understand.
A hug from the town where the man I love was born. Giulia"
